Charcoal data site locations

1 Introduction

Here we show the R code that we used to reproduce Matlab csaps() smoothing spline fit to the Allen Hills “long shapshot” in Shackleton et al. (2026), and to fit an alternative optimized smoothing spline in R. A smoothing splines is a cubic spline \(f\left(x_{i}\right)\) that is fit to some data \(y_{i}\) by minimizing a “penalized” residual sum-of-squares

\[ RSS\left(f,\lambda \right)=\{\textsf{goodness of fit}\}+\lambda\{\textsf{roughness}\} \]

The first term represents the goodness-of-fit of the spline curve to the data, while the second “penalty” term describes the rigidity or local variability of the curve. If λ = 0, the fitted spline simply interpolates between the \(y_{i}\)’s, while as λ → ∞ the penalty term increases and the optimal fitted curve becomes a least-squares straight line (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1990, p. 27).

The objective function used by the Matlab csaps() function is \[ RSS\left(f,\mathrm{\lambda }\right)=\left\{\ p\sum_{i=1}^{n} {w_{i}{\left(y_{i}-f\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}^{2}}+\left(1-p\right)\int {\left[f^{\prime \prime }\left(x\right)\right]}^{2}\,dx\right\} \]

Where \(f^{\prime \prime }\left(x\right)\) is the second derivative of the spline curve, and the \(w_{i}\)’s are possible weights for each data value, \(p\) is the user-selected smoothing parameter, and \(p=1/\left(1+\mathrm{\lambda }\right)\). When \(p=0\), a straight-line fit is obtained (i.e. as \(λ→∞\), \(p→0\)), while if \(λ=0\), then \(p=1\) and the spline \((f\left(x_{i}\right))\) simply interpolates between points.

The objective function for the R smooth.spline() function is \[ RSS\left(f,\lambda \right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} {w_{i}{\left(y_{i}-f\left(x_{i}\right)\right)}^{2}}+\lambda \int {{\left[f^{\prime \prime }\left(x\right)\right]}^{2}dx,} \]

Again, If \(λ=0\), the fitted spline simply interpolates between the \(y_{i}\)’s, while as \(λ→∞\) the penalty term increases and the optimal fitted curve becomes a least-squares straight line. The smoothing parameter is thus a measure of the “wiggliness” of the curve and can be set by a user at some fixed, scientifically based value, or it can be estimated by Generalized Cross Validation (GCV, Wahba, 1990, sec. 4.3) or some other approach. (GCV is a computationally efficient “leave-one-out” approach that is used to find an optimum trade-off between the goodness-of-fit and wigglyness of smoothing spline: an extremely smooth spline won’t fit the data very well, while an extremely wiggly spline can fit the data perfectly at the expense of being extremely non-smooth.) We use this approach below to obtain and “optimal” smoothing spline.

In the case of the R function, there are three ways of specifying or describing the amount of smoothing: via \(λ\); via a spar value, a scaleless description of the amount of smoothing which generally varies between 0 an 1; and via the equivalent degrees of freedom, \(df\) (Hastie and Tibshirani, 1990, sec. 3.5), a general measure of the amount of fitting done by the spline. Low values of \(df\) describe a fitted curve with fewer inflections while higher values describe a more wiggly curve.

Because the internal algorithms in the R and Matlab functions differ, there is no direct conversion between the methods (i.e. selecting the same value of \(λ\) for both will not yield equivalent results). The R function can nevertheless be used to approximate the results of applying the Matlab function by iteratively varying the spar parameter, and minimizing the sum-of-squared differences between the R- and Matlab-fitted smoothing splines. We use this approach below to approximate the results of from the Matlab csaps() using the R smooth.spline() functio

2 Read data

Load the neccessary packages. {readxl} and {writexl} read and write Excel files, {Hmisc} adds supplemental tick marks and plots, and {matrixStats} is used to get the bootstrap confidence itervals.

library(readxl, writexl)
library(Hmisc)
library(matrixStats)

Read the Allen Hills “long” snapshot data, and add 0.5 °C to account for the bias in the MOT anomalies.

# Allen_Hills_long data
# columns Q, X, Y and Z from the "Data Summary" tab of AllanHills_XeKr_temp-recon_2026-pubData-2.xlsx
data_path <- "~/Projects/globalT/MOT_Splines/data/"
file_name <- "AH_long.xlsx" 
xlxs_file <- paste(data_path, file_name, sep = "")
AH_long <- read_excel(xlxs_file)
head(AH_long); tail(AH_long)

leg_label <- paste("Spline from Shackleton et al. 2026 (Fig. 1)", sep="")
legend(3.5, -2.75, legend=c(leg_label), col="blue", lwd=2, bty="n")

3 Set-up tasks

Set target points for fitted splines:

# target pts for fitted spline
nsamp <- length(unique(AH_long$AgeMa))
age_max <- max(AH_long$AgeMa)
age_min <- min(AH_long$AgeMa)
x_targ <- seq(age_min, age_max, by = 0.005)
head(x_targ); tail(x_targ)
## [1] 0.430 0.435 0.440 0.445 0.450 0.455
## [1] 3.035 3.040 3.045 3.050 3.055 3.060
nfits <- length(x_targ)
nfits
## [1] 527

Set weights. weights weigh each observation by its uncertainty. ones weigh each observation equally

# weights
weights <- 1/(AH_long$MOT_abs_err^2)
ones = rep(1, length(AH_long$AgeMa))

Set parameters for bootstrap estimates of uncertainty

# bootstrap estimates of fitted values
set.seed(1234)
nreps <- 10000

Three curves will be fit here: 1) the approximation of the Shackleton et al. spline, 2) a GCV-optimized spine, and 3) and OLS linear fit. Define arrays and vectors to hold results:

ncurves <- 3

# arrays and vectors
fits <- matrix(0, nrow = nsamp, ncol = ncurves)
residuals <- matrix(0, nrow = nsamp, ncol = ncurves)
fits_bootstrap <- matrix(0, nrow=nfits, ncol = nreps)
df <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
lambda <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
rss <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
tss <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
sigma2 <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
AIC <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
rsq <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
adj_rsq <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))
F <- as.numeric(rep(0, ncurves))

model_colors <- c("black", "purple", "red")

4 Reproduce the Matlab smoothing spline with the R smoothing spline

The R smooth.spline() equivalent of the Matlab csaps() spline in Shackleton et al. can be estimated by repeated fitting splines with different values of the span parameter, ranging from 0.0 to 2.0 by 0.1:

# brute-force optinmization of spar value
npts <- 201
spar_opt <- as.numeric(seq(0.0, 2.0, by = 0.01))
df_opt <- as.numeric(rep(0, npts))
lambda_opt <- as.numeric(rep(0, npts))
rss_opt <- as.numeric(rep(0, npts))
tss_opt <- as.numeric(rep(0, npts))
rsq_opt <- as.numeric(rep(0, npts))

for (k in 1:npts) {
  curve_01 <- smooth.spline(AH_long$AgeMa, AH_long$MOT_anomaly, w = ones, spar = spar_opt[k])
  df_opt[k] <- curve_01$df; lambda_opt[k] <- curve_01$lambda
  
  y_pred <- predict(curve_01, AH_long_spline_paper$AgeMa, deriv = 0)$y
  resid <- y_pred - (AH_long_spline_paper$MOT_anomaly)
  rss_opt[k] <- sum(resid^2 )
  tss_opt[k] <- sum((AH_long_spline_paper$MOT_anomaly - mean(AH_long_spline_paper$MOT_anomaly))^2)
  rsq_opt[k] <- 1.0 - (rss_opt[k]/tss_opt[k])
}

Which value of spar produces the best fit?

match_paper <- data.frame(spar_opt, df_opt, lambda_opt, rss_opt, tss_opt, rsq_opt)
k_opt <- which.max(rsq_opt)
print(k_opt)
## [1] 70
print(match_paper[k_opt, ])
##    spar_opt  df_opt   lambda_opt   rss_opt  tss_opt  rsq_opt
## 70     0.69 12.4969 5.544198e-05 0.2163786 219.8993 0.999016

A spar value of 0.69 produces the best fit to published spline.

Refit the approximated spline and calculate the bootstrap confidence limits (while suppressing the individual fitted splines).

# Shackleton et al. spline

spar <- 0.69
curve_01 <- smooth.spline(AH_long$AgeMa, AH_long$MOT_anomaly, w = ones, 
    spar = spar, keep.stuff = TRUE) # Shackleton et al. specs. for lambda
y_pred_curve_01 <- predict(curve_01, x_targ, deriv = 0)$y
y_d1_curve_01 <- predict(curve_01, x_targ, deriv = 1)$y
y_d2_curve_01 <- predict(curve_01, x_targ, deriv = 2)$y
df[1] <- curve_01$df; lambda[1] <- curve_01$lambda; fits[, 1] <- curve_01$y
residuals[, 1] <- AH_long$MOT_anomaly - curve_01$y
sigma2[1] <- sum(residuals[, 1]^2)/(nsamp - 1.0)
rss[1] <- sum(residuals[, 1]^2 )
tss[1] <- sum((AH_long$MOT_anomaly - mean(AH_long$MOT_anomaly))^2)
# http://users.stat.umn.edu/~helwig/notes/smooth-spline-notes.html#aic-and-bic
max_log_lik <- (-1.0 / (2.0 * sigma2[1])) * rss[1] - 1.0 * (nsamp / 2.0) * log(sigma2[1]) - 
  1.0 * (nsamp / 2.0) * log(2 * pi)
AIC[1] <- - 2.0 * max_log_lik + 2.0 * df[1]
AIC[1] <- round(AIC[1], 2)
print(AIC[1])
## [1] 84.92
# R-sq values
rsq[1] <- 1 - (rss[1]/tss[1])
adj_rsq[1] <- 1 - (rss[1] / (nsamp - df[1])) / (tss[1] / (nsamp - 1))
rsq[1] <- round(rsq[1], digits = 3)
adj_rsq[1] <- round(adj_rsq[1], digits = 3)
rsq[1]; adj_rsq[1]
## [1] 0.759
## [1] 0.715
# bootsrap CL's -- calculate but do not plot
fits_bootstrap <- matrix(0, nrow=nfits, ncol = nreps)
k <- 0; j <- 1
for (i in 1:nreps) {
  # print(i)
  x_boot <- AH_long$AgeMa + rnorm(nsamp, mean = 0, sd = AH_long$Rel_err_Myr)
  x_boot <- x_boot[order(x_boot)]
  y_boot <- AH_long$MOT_anomaly + rnorm(nsamp, mean = 0, sd = AH_long$MOT_abs_err)
  y_boot <- y_boot[order(x_boot)]
  # points(x_boot, y_boot, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
  
  fit_boot <- smooth.spline(x_boot, y_boot, w = ones, spar = spar ) # df = df[1])
  if (length(x_boot) == length(fit_boot$y)) {
    y_pred <- predict(fit_boot, x_targ, deriv = 0)$y
    # if (i < 500) {
    #   lines(x_targ, y_pred, col=adjustcolor(model_colors[j], alpha = 0.05))
    #   # points(AH_long$AgeMa, y_pred, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
    # }
    k <- k + 1
    fits_bootstrap[1:nfits, k] <- y_pred[1:nfits]
  }
}

# get the various quantiles of the fitted splines
boot_cl_01 <- rowQuantiles(fits_bootstrap, probs = c(0.025, 0.16, 0.50, 0.84, 0.975))
head(boot_cl_01)
